title: Temperature and Diversity: How Sampling Parameters Affect Lean 4 Proof Generation

original_idea.body:
# Temperature and Diversity: How Sampling Parameters Affect Lean 4 Proof Generation

**Problem:** LLM sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, number of samples) significantly affect code generation quality. Their impact on formal proof generation success in Lean 4 is not systematically studied.

**Direction:** Run grid search over temperature (0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0) and sample count (1, 5, 10, 50) on VeriBench using Claude/GPT-4/Leanstral. Measure compilation rate, proof success rate, and diversity of proof strategies. Find optimal configuration.

**Why it matters:** Formal verification is expensive. Understanding the sample-efficiency tradeoff could dramatically reduce compute requirements for reaching target success rates, making LLM-assisted verification economically viable.

**Relevant context:** LLM sampling for code generation is well-studied (pass@k metrics). This has not been applied to Lean 4 formal proof generation. The Self-Optimizing Trace Agent implicitly uses multiple samples but does not report parameter sensitivity.

title: Task Difficulty Scaling in Lean 4: Does Proof Complexity Predict LLM Failure?

original_idea.body:
# Task Difficulty Scaling in Lean 4: Does Proof Complexity Predict LLM Failure?

**Problem:** VeriBench contains easy, medium, and hard Lean 4 tasks. The relationship between task complexity (proof length, number of lemmas, logical depth) and LLM failure rate is not characterized.

**Direction:** Compute structural complexity metrics for each VeriBench task (proof length in reference solution, dependency depth, number of auxiliary lemmas, cyclomatic complexity). Correlate these with LLM compilation and proof success rates across models.

**Why it matters:** If complexity predicts failure, simple complexity metrics could serve as a proxy for 'this task requires human verification expert review' — a practical triage tool for deployment.

**Relevant context:** IRT and psychometric approaches (from prior work on AI benchmark calibration) could be applied to Lean 4 benchmark tasks. No difficulty calibration exists for formal verification benchmarks.

title: Language Transfer for Vericoding: Does Lean Performance Predict Dafny Performance?

original_idea.body:
# Language Transfer for Vericoding: Does Lean Performance Predict Dafny Performance?

**Problem:** AlphaVerus transfers from Dafny to Verus. Mistral's Leanstral targets Lean 4. Whether LLM performance at formal verification transfers across languages (Lean 4, Dafny, Verus, Coq, Isabelle) is unknown.

**Direction:** Take 30 benchmark problems with gold solutions in multiple proof languages. Measure LLM success rate per language for the same problem. Compute cross-language rank correlation. Test whether Lean performance predicts Dafny performance.

**Why it matters:** If performance transfers across proof languages, a single benchmark suffices. If not, each language needs its own evaluation infrastructure, and organizations cannot compare claims across systems.

**Relevant context:** VeriCoding benchmark (POPL 2026) covers Lean, Rust/Verus, and Dafny. Multiple benchmarks now exist. Cross-language LLM performance comparison has not been done systematically.

title: Feedback Loop Quality: How Error Message Precision Affects Self-Correction in Lean 4

original_idea.body:
# Feedback Loop Quality: How Error Message Precision Affects Self-Correction in Lean 4

**Problem:** The Self-Optimizing Trace Agent uses Lean 4 compiler error messages to guide self-correction. Whether error message quality/verbosity affects correction success is untested.

**Direction:** Vary error message presentation to the LLM: (a) full compiler output, (b) summary only, (c) line number only, (d) no error message. Measure how many iterations are needed to reach compilation. Test on 50 VeriBench tasks.

**Why it matters:** Lean 4 compiler messages are notoriously verbose. Understanding how much information is needed for self-correction guides tool design for future AI-assisted verification pipelines.

**Relevant context:** Self-Optimizing Trace Agent architecture is documented in VeriBench (ICML 2025). Compiler feedback is a key component, but its informational sufficiency has not been tested.

title: Security Challenge vs. Algorithmic Problem: Differential LLM Capability at Lean 4 Security Proofs

original_idea.body:
# Security Challenge vs. Algorithmic Problem: Differential LLM Capability at Lean 4 Security Proofs

**Problem:** VeriBench includes 11 security challenge problems out of 113 total. Whether LLMs perform systematically worse on security-specific formal verification tasks compared to general algorithmic tasks at the same complexity level is unstudied.

**Direction:** Match security challenge problems to algorithmic problems of similar proof length and complexity from VeriBench. Run the same models on both sets. Measure performance gap. Collect qualitative error analysis of where security proof attempts fail.

**Why it matters:** A systematic gap in security-specific formal verification would indicate that improving LLM performance on general benchmarks does not transfer to the most safety-relevant use case.

**Relevant context:** VeriBench (ICML 2025) includes both categories. The 11 security challenges are a natural treatment group. This is a tractable comparison with available public benchmarks.

title: Model Size Scaling for Lean 4 Proof Generation: Does Bigger Always Mean Better?

original_idea.body:
# Model Size Scaling for Lean 4 Proof Generation: Does Bigger Always Mean Better?

**Problem:** LLM performance on formal verification at Lean 4 has been tested at limited model sizes. Whether performance scales predictably with model size (consistent with scaling laws) or exhibits unexpected capability jumps/plateaus is unknown.

**Direction:** Run VeriBench across model size families (7B, 13B, 34B, 70B parameters for open models; Claude haiku/sonnet/opus variants) and fit scaling curves. Test whether Lean 4 proof capability follows a smooth power law or shows capability emergence.

**Why it matters:** If formal verification capability emerges abruptly at some scale threshold, safety planning based on capability projections may be wrong. Identifying the scaling regime is important for forecasting when AI-assisted formal verification becomes deployment-ready.

**Relevant context:** LLaMA-70B fails to compile any Lean programs in VeriBench (0%), while Claude 3.7 Sonnet achieves 12.5%. This suggests a non-smooth scaling pattern worth investigating.

title: Explaining the 60% vs. 12.5% Gap: What Does the Self-Optimizing Trace Agent Do Differently?

original_idea.body:
# Explaining the 60% vs. 12.5% Gap: What Does the Self-Optimizing Trace Agent Do Differently?

**Problem:** The Self-Optimizing Trace Agent jumps from a 12.5% baseline to ~60% compilation rate on Lean 4. The exact mechanisms responsible for this surprising improvement are not well characterized in the original paper.

**Direction:** Reverse-engineer the agent's behavior by analyzing its trace logs: (1) what fraction of successful proofs required multiple iterations, (2) what types of compiler errors are successfully corrected, (3) what fraction of proofs succeed on first attempt. Build a taxonomy of the agent's correction strategies.

**Why it matters:** Understanding what the 60% figure actually represents (whether it is multi-attempt success at easy problems or genuine capability on hard problems) is critical for interpreting the result as a safety signal.

**Relevant context:** VeriBench (ICML 2025) documents the 60% figure. The agent architecture uses trace-based self-optimization, but the mechanism responsible for the improvement is not dissected in the paper.

title: Does the 60% Compilation Rate Generalize to Real-World Code? Testing Self-Optimizing Trace Agent on Unseen Codebases

# Does the 60% Compilation Rate Generalize to Real-World Code? Testing Self-Optimizing Trace Agent on Unseen Codebases

**Problem:** The Self-Optimizing Trace Agent achieves 60% on VeriBench benchmarks (many derived from HumanEval). Whether this rate generalizes to real-world, non-benchmark code is a critical follow-up question.

**Direction:** Apply the Self-Optimizing Trace Agent to 50 functions sampled from real open-source Python/Rust codebases (not in any benchmark). Measure compilation rate and compare to the 60% figure. Identify what properties of benchmark problems make them easier than real code.

**Why it matters:** If the 60% rate is benchmark-specific and drops dramatically on real code, the gap between AI formal verification capability and real-world deployment remains larger than reported.

**Relevant context:** HumanEval-derived benchmarks are known to be simpler than production code. VeriBench explicitly notes it begins with HumanEval problems. Generalization to real code is the RAND report's key concern.

title: Claude Found 500+ Vulnerabilities — What Types? A Systematic Taxonomy

original_idea.body:
# Claude Found 500+ Vulnerabilities — What Types? A Systematic Taxonomy

**Problem:** Anthropic's Claude Code Security found 500+ production vulnerabilities undetected for decades. Whether these are clustered in specific vulnerability categories (memory safety, logic bugs, injection, cryptographic) is not publicly characterized.

**Direction:** Analyze the public disclosure list from Claude Code Security (Anthropic 2026). Classify each vulnerability by CWE category, age, affected programming language, and detection method required. Compare distribution to CVE database baseline to identify which types semantic reasoning finds that pattern matching misses.

**Why it matters:** If the 500+ vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific categories, formal verification benchmarks should prioritize those categories. The taxonomy would directly inform benchmark design and safety tool development.

**Relevant context:** Claude Code Security (Anthropic 2026) found vulnerabilities including zero-days in OpenSSL. The announcement exists but vulnerability categorization is not publicly analyzed in aggregate.

title: Does Self-Reflection Improve Formal Proof Generation? Testing Self-Critique Against External Verification

original_idea.body:
# Does Self-Reflection Improve Formal Proof Generation? Testing Self-Critique Against External Verification

**Problem:** Claude Code Security uses a multi-stage self-verification step to filter false positives. Whether AI self-reflection on Lean 4 proofs (spotting its own errors before submission) is effective is untested.

**Direction:** Compare two conditions on 50 VeriBench tasks: (a) model generates proof and submits directly, (b) model generates proof, critiques it, revises, then submits. Measure first-pass compilation rate and final success rate. Analyze what types of errors self-reflection catches.

**Why it matters:** If self-reflection significantly improves Lean 4 proof success, it could be a lightweight augmentation that does not require agentic loops. If it does not help, the overhead is unjustified.

**Relevant context:** Claude Code Security's multi-stage verification (Anthropic 2026) suggests self-reflection helps for vulnerability detection. AlphaVerus uses a Critique stage. Whether this transfers to formal proof generation is unstudied.

title: From 86% to 100%: What Structural Features Prevent Full Vulnerability Detection in DARPA AIxCC?

original_idea.body:
# From 86% to 100%: What Structural Features Prevent Full Vulnerability Detection in DARPA AIxCC?

**Problem:** DARPA AIxCC reached 77% vulnerability detection in the final round (up from 37%). The remaining 23% undetected vulnerabilities may have structural properties that resist both AI and formal methods approaches.

**Direction:** Analyze the AIxCC competition results. Collect examples of vulnerabilities that no system detected. Characterize their structural properties: are they multi-function, require domain knowledge, involve subtle protocol logic, or are they physically distributed across files? Test whether LLM-based formal specification can capture these properties.

**Why it matters:** The gap between 77% and 100% represents the hardest class of vulnerabilities. Understanding what formal or AI approach is needed to cover this gap is a key safety research question.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC SoK paper (arXiv 2602.07666) provides detailed competition analysis. 7 finalist teams with open-source systems will be released. The gap represents a concrete, measurable failure mode to characterize.

title: Iterative Proof Generation Failure Modes: Where Do LLMs Get Stuck in Lean 4?

original_idea.body:
# Iterative Proof Generation Failure Modes: Where Do LLMs Get Stuck in Lean 4?

**Problem:** When LLMs fail on Lean 4 tasks after multiple iterations, it is unclear whether they are making progress (getting closer to a valid proof) or cycling without convergence. Understanding the failure dynamics matters for when to give up.

**Direction:** Run 10-iteration traces on 30 VeriBench tasks that fail to compile. At each iteration, measure: (a) number of compiler errors, (b) error type distribution, (c) proof fragment similarity to previous attempt. Classify failures as: converging, cycling, regressing.

**Why it matters:** Iterative agents need stopping criteria. If most failures cycle rather than converge, exponential compute waste can be avoided by early termination. This has direct implications for the cost-efficiency of agentic verification pipelines.

**Relevant context:** Self-Optimizing Trace Agent uses multiple iterations. The agent behavior on failures is not characterized. ATLAS pipeline also uses iterative synthesis, but failure dynamics are not analyzed.

title: Replicating VeriBench Results on Mistral Leanstral: First Open-Source Lean 4 Agent Evaluation

original_idea.body:
# Replicating VeriBench Results on Mistral Leanstral: First Open-Source Lean 4 Agent Evaluation

**Problem:** Mistral released Leanstral (March 2026) as the first open-source Lean 4 proof agent. Its performance relative to closed-source models on VeriBench has not been systematically evaluated.

**Direction:** Replicate the VeriBench evaluation protocol using Leanstral. Compare its compilation rate, proof success rate, and error distribution to the published numbers for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and the Self-Optimizing Trace Agent. Document any discrepancies from replication.

**Why it matters:** Leanstral being open-source enables reproducibility research and community iteration. Establishing its baseline is a prerequisite for all subsequent improvement work. If it underperforms closed models significantly, it pinpoints where open-source formal verification falls short.

**Relevant context:** Mistral Leanstral was released March 16, 2026. VeriBench is publicly available on OpenReview. This is a straightforward replication study that fills an important gap in the literature.

title: AlphaVerus on Lean 4: Does CMU's Self-Improving Translation Approach Transfer to a Different Proof Language?

original_idea.body:
# AlphaVerus on Lean 4: Does CMU's Self-Improving Translation Approach Transfer to a Different Proof Language?

**Problem:** AlphaVerus achieves 38% success on HumanEval-Verified by translating from Dafny to Verus. Whether the same self-improving translation approach works when the target is Lean 4 instead of Verus is untested.

**Direction:** Implement an AlphaVerus-style pipeline (Exploration, Treefinement, Critique stages) but targeting Lean 4 instead of Verus. Run on the HumanEval-Verified subset. Compare to the original 38% Verus result. Identify where Lean 4's type theory creates additional challenges.

**Why it matters:** Lean 4 is the primary target for CSLib and the AI safety formal methods community. If AlphaVerus-style bootstrapping transfers to Lean 4, it provides a training data generation strategy for the data-scarce domain.

**Relevant context:** AlphaVerus (CMU 2024) is open-source. Lean 4 is more expressive than Verus but has more complex type theory. CSLib targets Lean 4. The translation from Dafny→Verus could be adapted to Dafny→Lean 4.

title: ATLAS Pipeline Replication on Security-Specific Programs: Does Scale Transfer to Security Domains?

original_idea.body:
# ATLAS Pipeline Replication on Security-Specific Programs: Does Scale Transfer to Security Domains?

**Problem:** ATLAS (POPL 2026) synthesizes 2.7K verified Dafny programs at scale. Whether this pipeline produces reliable verified programs when applied specifically to security-critical algorithms (cryptographic, access control, input validation) is untested.

**Direction:** Run the ATLAS pipeline restricted to a seed set of security-relevant function descriptions (crypto primitives, bounds checkers, input sanitizers). Compare verification success rate to ATLAS's reported rate on general programs. Manually audit 20 outputs for security property correctness.

**Why it matters:** The RAND report calls for security-specific benchmarks. ATLAS could generate them at scale, but only if it works in this domain. This replication directly addresses the benchmark gap identified by RAND.

**Relevant context:** ATLAS code and methodology are from POPL 2026. Dafny has good support for security reasoning. This is a targeted domain replication of an established methodology.

title: AIxCC Vulnerability Detection Methodology on a New Language Ecosystem: Does Java Performance Match C?

original_idea.body:
# AIxCC Vulnerability Detection Methodology on a New Language Ecosystem: Does Java Performance Match C?

**Problem:** AIxCC final round found 6 vulnerabilities in C and 12 in Java codebases. Whether the same AI Cyber Reasoning System architectures perform better in Java than C (or vice versa) due to language ecosystem differences has not been examined.

**Direction:** Replicate AIxCC-style vulnerability detection using open-source finalist system architectures on a balanced test set of C and Java vulnerabilities from CVE database. Measure detection rate per language. Characterize language-specific failure modes.

**Why it matters:** If detection rates differ significantly by language, language-specific formal verification tooling may be needed. This informs where formal methods investment will have the highest safety impact.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC SoK paper (arXiv 2602.07666) shows 6 C vs 12 Java findings. Finalist systems will be open-sourced in August 2025. Language-specific performance analysis is a natural follow-up.

# Lean 4 Security Benchmark: A Curated Dataset of Formally Specifiable Security Properties

**Problem:** No benchmark exists for evaluating AI's ability to generate formally verified Lean 4 code specifically for security-critical tasks (buffer overflows, injection vulnerabilities, cryptographic correctness). VeriBench's 11 security examples are insufficient.

**Direction:** Construct a benchmark of 100 security-critical coding tasks with formal Lean 4 specifications covering: memory safety, integer overflow, SQL injection prevention, cryptographic constant-time requirements, access control logic. Write reference solutions. Measure current LLM baseline performance.

**Why it matters:** RAND (Sarma & Fisher 2026) explicitly calls for security-focused formal verification benchmarks. Without one, progress toward safe AI-generated security code cannot be measured. This directly fills the gap they identify.

**Relevant context:** VeriBench has 11 security challenges. CLEVER benchmark (arXiv 2505.13938) focuses on general correctness. No benchmark targets security properties specifically in Lean 4. CSLib's roadmap does not include security examples.

title: VeriSpec: A Benchmark for AI Specification Writing Quality in Formal Verification
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# VeriSpec: A Benchmark for AI Specification Writing Quality in Formal Verification

**Problem:** Current benchmarks (VeriBench, CLEVER, VeriCoding) evaluate whether LLMs can complete a proof given a specification. No benchmark evaluates whether LLMs can write correct, non-trivial specifications from natural language requirements.

**Direction:** Create a benchmark of 80 natural language function requirements paired with expert-written formal specifications. LLMs must generate formal specs. Evaluate: (a) syntactic correctness, (b) semantic completeness against expert spec, (c) non-triviality (not vacuously true). Establish baseline metrics.

**Why it matters:** Specification writing is the hardest and most safety-critical part of formal verification. If LLMs cannot write correct specs, the entire verified code generation pipeline fails at its foundation.

**Relevant context:** ATLAS (POPL 2026) generates specs automatically but does not validate spec quality against intent. VeriEquivBench (arXiv 2510.06296) measures equivalence. Spec quality as a standalone evaluation is missing.

title: FormalBench-CSLib: A Benchmark Aligned to CSLib's 2026 Algorithm Coverage

# FormalBench-CSLib: A Benchmark Aligned to CSLib's 2026 Algorithm Coverage

**Problem:** CSLib plans to cover undergraduate algorithms and data structures by end of 2026. No benchmark exists to evaluate AI's ability to generate formally verified implementations specifically for this CSLib coverage set.

**Direction:** Create a benchmark of 60 algorithm problems (sorting, searching, graph traversal, data structures) aligned to CSLib's planned coverage. For each, provide: natural language description, Python reference implementation, and expert Lean 4 specification. Measure current LLM performance as a baseline.

**Why it matters:** This benchmark would directly track progress toward one of the most concrete near-term formal methods milestones (CSLib completion) and would enable the community to measure whether AI assistance accelerates CSLib development.

**Relevant context:** CSLib roadmap (arXiv 2602.04846) details 2026 targets. No benchmark is aligned to this roadmap. This would create infrastructure for measuring AI contribution to CSLib completion.

title: Proof Complexity Metric Library: Automated Difficulty Estimation for Lean 4 Tasks

original_idea.body:
# Proof Complexity Metric Library: Automated Difficulty Estimation for Lean 4 Tasks

**Problem:** No standardized metric library exists for estimating the difficulty of Lean 4 formal verification tasks from source code properties. Benchmark designers must manually classify difficulty.

**Direction:** Build a Python library that, given a Lean 4 problem, computes: (a) proof length in reference solution, (b) number of auxiliary lemmas, (c) dependency graph depth, (d) number of unique tactics used, (e) abstraction level. Validate that these metrics correlate with LLM success rates on VeriBench.

**Why it matters:** Automated difficulty estimation enables principled benchmark design, adaptive evaluation systems, and fair comparison across models. Without it, benchmark composition choices are ad hoc.

**Relevant context:** IRT-based difficulty estimation has been applied to NLP benchmarks but not to formal verification. VeriBench and CLEVER have difficulty tiers but do not compute them automatically. This is a tooling gap.

title: AI-Assisted Proof Debugging Tool: Localizing Lean 4 Errors to Source Intentions

original_idea.body:
# AI-Assisted Proof Debugging Tool: Localizing Lean 4 Errors to Source Intentions

**Problem:** When Lean 4 proof attempts fail, compiler error messages are verbose but not always actionable. No tool exists to map Lean 4 compiler errors back to the LLM's apparent proof strategy to explain why the strategy is failing.

**Direction:** Build a lightweight tool that: (a) parses Lean 4 compiler errors, (b) uses an LLM to generate a natural language explanation of which proof step failed and why, (c) suggests the nearest valid alternative tactic. Evaluate usefulness with 10 CS students attempting Lean proofs.

**Why it matters:** Better error explanation tools would accelerate LLM self-correction and human-in-the-loop verification workflows. This is a prerequisite for making formal verification accessible to non-experts.

**Relevant context:** Self-Optimizing Trace Agent relies on error messages for self-correction. Lean 4's error messages are known to be cryptic (noted in multiple formal verification papers). No LLM-based error explainer for Lean 4 exists.

title: Verified Patch Benchmark: Does AI-Generated Security Patch Actually Fix the Vulnerability?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Verified Patch Benchmark: Does AI-Generated Security Patch Actually Fix the Vulnerability?

**Problem:** AIxCC systems detected vulnerabilities and generated patches, but patch correctness verification was manual. No benchmark exists for formally verifying that a security patch eliminates the target vulnerability without introducing regressions.

**Direction:** Create a benchmark of 40 (vulnerability, patch) pairs from the AIxCC competition and public CVE disclosures. For each pair, attempt to write Lean 4/Dafny specifications that prove: (a) the patch eliminates the vulnerable behavior, (b) the original functionality is preserved. Measure LLM success rate on each task.

**Why it matters:** Automated patch verification is the missing link between vulnerability detection and confident remediation. If AI can both find and formally verify a patch, the security loop closes without human proof review.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC patched 61% of detected vulnerabilities. Patch correctness was validated by re-running tests, not formal proofs. AIxCC open-source release scheduled for August 2025 provides the data.

title: Multi-Language Formal Verification Consistency Checker: Detecting Semantic Divergence Across Proof Languages
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Language Formal Verification Consistency Checker: Detecting Semantic Divergence Across Proof Languages

**Problem:** A program can be formally verified in Lean 4, Dafny, and Coq with proofs that appear equivalent but encode different semantic assumptions. No tool exists to cross-validate proofs across proof languages for the same program.

**Direction:** Build a tool that: (a) takes a function with proofs in two languages, (b) extracts the semantic content of each proof's core theorem, (c) uses an LLM to judge whether the theorems are semantically equivalent, (d) flags divergences. Test on 20 programs with gold proofs in two languages.

**Why it matters:** For safety-critical applications, proof consistency across multiple verification systems provides higher assurance. Cross-language consistency checking is an unbuilt tool in the verification toolchain.

**Relevant context:** VeriCoding benchmark covers Lean, Verus, and Dafny. AlphaVerus translates between them. No tool validates semantic equivalence of cross-language proofs. This is a gap in verification tooling.

title: Lean 4 Proof Failure Taxonomy: Systematic Classification of LLM Formal Verification Errors

original_idea.body:
# Lean 4 Proof Failure Taxonomy: Systematic Classification of LLM Formal Verification Errors

**Problem:** When LLMs fail at Lean 4 formal verification, error types are classified loosely (compilation error, type error, proof incomplete) but no systematic taxonomy exists for what logical reasoning failures produce which error patterns.

**Direction:** Collect 300 failed Lean 4 proof attempts from public datasets and LLM runs on VeriBench. Manually code each failure into a taxonomy (type mismatch, wrong induction hypothesis, missing lemma, incomplete case analysis, wrong tactic order, etc.). Compute inter-rater reliability. Release as a labeled dataset.

**Why it matters:** A systematic failure taxonomy enables targeted improvement: if 40% of failures involve wrong induction hypotheses, training methods can specifically address that. Without taxonomy, improvement is undirected.

**Relevant context:** Lean 4 failure modes are mentioned qualitatively in VeriBench and BRIDGE papers but never systematically categorized. DARPA AIxCC SoK provides a model for systematic failure analysis that could be adapted.

title: Vacuous Proof Failure Mode: How Often Do LLMs Prove True but Useless Properties in Lean 4?

original_idea.body:
# Vacuous Proof Failure Mode: How Often Do LLMs Prove True but Useless Properties in Lean 4?

**Problem:** A specific and dangerous failure mode in formal verification is generating proofs that are syntactically valid but prove vacuously true or trivially weak properties — giving false safety assurance.

**Direction:** Run 5 LLMs on 60 VeriBench tasks. For all generated proofs that compile successfully, have an expert Lean user classify each as: (a) proves the stated property correctly, (b) proves a weaker/vacuous variant of the property, (c) the property itself is trivially satisfiable. Measure vacuity rate.

**Why it matters:** Vacuous proofs are invisible to automated compilation checking — they are the most dangerous class of false assurance in formal verification. If vacuity rates are high, compilation-rate benchmarks significantly overstate actual safety assurance.

**Relevant context:** Vacuity detection is an active research area in model checking. It is not addressed in current Lean 4 LLM evaluation. VeriBench does not filter for vacuous proofs. This is a critical but uninvestigated failure mode.

title: Specification Underspecification: When AI-Generated Lean Proofs Miss Important Edge Cases
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Specification Underspecification: When AI-Generated Lean Proofs Miss Important Edge Cases

**Problem:** LLM-generated Lean specifications systematically omit edge cases (empty inputs, overflow boundaries, null/None values), producing proofs valid only for common-case inputs. This failure mode is not characterized.

**Direction:** Take 40 VeriBench problems with known edge cases. Generate Lean specs and proofs with 3 LLMs. For each successful proof, construct edge-case test inputs and run them through the verified program. Measure how often the formally verified program still fails on edge cases.

**Why it matters:** A program can be formally verified and still crash on edge-case inputs if the spec omits those edge cases. This failure mode undermines the safety claims of vericoding for real applications.

**Relevant context:** CLEVER benchmark (arXiv 2505.13938) focuses on curated correctness but does not specifically test edge case coverage. This is a known weakness in test-driven development that may carry over to formal verification.

title: Proof Hallucination Under Distribution Shift: Formal Verification on Modified Code
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped to specific AI safety failure mode with clear measurement methodology

original_idea.body:
# Proof Hallucination Under Distribution Shift: Formal Verification on Modified Code

**Problem:** When code is modified slightly (renaming variables, reordering functions, adding dead code), LLM-generated proofs may fail catastrophically even though the logical content is unchanged. This distributional fragility is a safety-relevant failure mode.

**Direction:** Take 30 VeriBench problems with working LLM-generated proofs. Apply semantic-preserving transformations (variable rename, function reorder, dead code injection). Measure proof success rate degradation. Identify which transformations cause the most failures.

**Why it matters:** If formal verification is fragile to surface-level code changes, it cannot be used as a robust safety check in real development workflows where code is constantly evolving.

**Relevant context:** LLM robustness to syntactic variation is studied in code generation. In formal verification, this robustness question has not been investigated. The failure mode would indicate proofs are surface-level pattern matching rather than deep reasoning.

title: The 23% Gap in AIxCC: Structural Analysis of Undetected Vulnerabilities

original_idea.body:
# The 23% Gap in AIxCC: Structural Analysis of Undetected Vulnerabilities

**Problem:** AIxCC reached 77% vulnerability detection but 23% went undetected. This gap likely represents structurally distinct vulnerability classes that resist both AI semantic reasoning and automated formal methods.

**Direction:** From the AIxCC SoK paper and open-source release, identify examples of undetected vulnerabilities. Classify by: (a) structural type (inter-procedural, concurrency, cryptographic, configuration), (b) language, (c) detection approach required. Test whether LLM+formal verification hybrid could detect them.

**Why it matters:** The 23% undetected class is the highest-value target for improving AI-assisted security. Understanding its structure enables focused tool development. This directly advances the RAND goal of tipping cyber balance toward defense.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC SoK paper (arXiv 2602.07666) provides detailed competition analysis. Finalist systems to be open-sourced. The 23% gap is a concrete, measurable failure set to characterize.

title: Inconsistency Between Verified Spec and Runtime Behavior: A Measurement Study
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Inconsistency Between Verified Spec and Runtime Behavior: A Measurement Study

**Problem:** Even when Lean 4 proofs are valid, the verified program may behave differently at runtime due to implementation details not captured in the Lean model (integer semantics, floating point, I/O behavior). Measuring this gap is unstudied.

**Direction:** Take 25 programs with complete Lean 4 proofs. Compile them to execution via Lean's extraction or equivalent. Run 1000 randomized inputs per program. Measure how often runtime behavior contradicts the formally verified property (e.g., via assertion violations in property-checked versions).

**Why it matters:** The gap between the formal model and executable reality is where safety guarantees break down. If this gap is large, formal verification provides weaker safety guarantees than commonly assumed.

**Relevant context:** Lean 4 programs can be extracted and run. The Curry-Howard correspondence is exact at the proof level but execution semantics differ. This failure mode is known in Coq/Isabelle extraction but unstudied for Lean 4 LLM-generated proofs.

title: Importing Software Model Checking into Lean 4: CBMC-Guided Proof Generation

original_idea.body:
# Importing Software Model Checking into Lean 4: CBMC-Guided Proof Generation

**Problem:** CBMC (C Bounded Model Checker) can automatically prove absence of specific bug classes in bounded C programs. These verification certificates could guide Lean 4 proof construction but this cross-tool integration does not exist.

**Direction:** For 30 C programs with CBMC verification certificates, attempt to import the CBMC proof structure into Lean 4 as a proof scaffold. Measure whether LLMs can complete the Lean proof using CBMC output as structured hints. Compare to unaided LLM proof attempts.

**Why it matters:** CBMC produces machine-checkable certificates for C programs. Bridging CBMC to Lean 4 would allow formally verified C code to feed into the CSLib ecosystem, creating a pathway from legacy code to formally verified library entries.

**Relevant context:** CBMC is a mature industrial tool (Amazon uses it for AWS). Lean 4 is the target for CSLib. No bridge between bounded model checking certificates and Lean 4 proofs exists. DARPA AIxCC used CBMC-style techniques.
